chapter_note.about: Linear regression draws the straight line that sits closest to a cloud of points. "Closest" means the smallest total of squared vertical gaps, called the SSE. For one feature there are two short formulas: one for a line through the origin and one for a line with an intercept. GATE asks you to apply them by hand on three or four points, and then to reason about the line: the residuals add to zero, R-squared, how many weights there are, and what changes when you rescale. It has also asked a single gradient-descent step.

chapter_note.simple: Linear regression is about drawing the best straight line through a cloud of dots. "Best" means the line whose up-and-down misses, squared and added, are as small as possible. You can find that line with a couple of averages: it goes through the average dot, and its steepness comes from how x and y move together. Once you have a line you can score it with R-squared, check it because its misses add up to zero, and see what happens when you change units or add more columns. When there are many columns the same idea is written as one matrix equation, and there is also a slower, general way to find the line by taking small downhill steps.

cards.title: Residual and SSE
cards.simple: Lay a ruler across a scatter of dots on a graph. Every dot sits a little above or below the ruler, and that up-or-down gap is its miss. To score the ruler, square each miss and add them up. Squaring makes ups and downs both count as bad, and it makes one wide miss cost more than several small ones, like a bowler who is punished more for one wild wide than for a few slightly loose balls. The ruler with the smallest score is the best line. In exam words: residual = actual minus predicted, SSE = sum of squared residuals, and least squares picks the line with the smallest SSE.
cards.idea: You have a handful of dots on a graph and want one straight line that passes as close to them as possible. For each dot, measure the vertical gap between the dot and the line. That gap is a **residual**. Square every gap and add the squares. The line with the smallest total wins.
cards.definition:
For a point with actual value $y$ and a line that predicts $\hat y$ at the same $x$:

$$e=y-\hat y,\qquad \text{SSE}=\sum_i e_i^2$$

Symbols: $e$ is the residual. $\hat y$ (read "y hat") is the prediction. $\sum_i$ means "add this up over every point $i$". A dot above the line has $e>0$, and a dot below has $e<0$. Least squares chooses the line with the smallest possible SSE.
cards.intuition_full: Picture each dot joined to the line by a rubber band that pulls straight up or down. A band stretched twice as far stores four times the energy, and squaring does the same thing to a gap. The line settles where the total stretch energy is lowest. Squaring does three jobs. It makes every miss positive, so +1 and -1 cannot cancel. It charges big misses extra, so the line will not leave one dot far away. And it gives a smooth bowl-shaped total, so setting its slope to zero finds the bottom exactly, which is how the formulas in the next cards are found. The sum of absolute gaps is also a fair score, but it gives a different line and has no neat formula. You can also draw a real square on each gap. SSE is then the total area of the squares, and the best line makes that area as small as possible.

example.setup: Four points: (1,1), (2,2), (3,2), (4,5). Score the line $\hat y=x$, then compare it with the line $\hat y=1.2x-0.5$.
steps: SSE $=0+0+1+1=2$. The plain sum of the residuals is $0+0-1+1=0$, which would wrongly call this line perfect.
Now try $\hat y=1.2x-0.5$. It predicts $0.7,\ 1.9,\ 3.1,\ 4.3$, so the residuals are $0.3,\ 0.1,\ -1.1,\ 0.7$.
SSE $=0.09+0.01+1.21+0.49=1.8$. That is smaller than 2, so the second line is better.
example.answer: SSE is 2 for $\hat y=x$ and 1.8 for $\hat y=1.2x-0.5$. The second line is in fact the least-squares line for these points.

cards.why: Every regression question starts from the residual. SSE is the score that least squares minimises, and ridge and logistic regression just change this score. In GATE: you are given points and a line and must find a residual or the SSE by hand, or say which quantity least squares minimises.
how: For each point, plug $x$ into the line to get the prediction $\hat y$.
Residual = actual minus predicted. Keep the sign for now.
Square every residual so none is negative.
Add the squares. That total is the SSE. Divide by the number of points for the MSE.
cards.mistake: Adding the signed residuals and calling that the error. Positive and negative gaps cancel, so a poor line can score 0. Square each gap first, then add.
edge_cases: All points exactly on the line: every residual is 0, so SSE = 0.
Flip the subtraction ($\hat y-y$ instead of $y-\hat y$) and every sign flips, but SSE stays the same.
SSE has the units of $y$ squared. Change $y$ from metres to centimetres and SSE grows $100^2=10{,}000$ times.
Least squares measures the gap straight up and down, not the shortest distance to the line.
connections: Foundations: Sequences and series. The sigma sign $\sum$ in SSE is explained there.
Ridge regression adds a penalty on the weights to this same SSE.
Logistic regression replaces SSE with log-loss, because its target is a class and not a number.

cards.title: Through-origin slope
cards.simple: Picture a ruler pinned to the corner (0,0) of the graph so it can only swing, never slide. You get to choose just one thing: how steep it is. Multiply each x by its y and add those up. Then square each x and add those up. The best steepness is the first total divided by the second. Think of every dot as voting for the slope it would like, with dots far from the pin getting a louder vote. In exam words: for $y=wx$ the least-squares slope is $w=\sum xy/\sum x^2$.
cards.idea: Suppose the line must pass through the origin, so its equation is $\hat y=wx$ with no intercept. Only one number is free: the slope $w$. Each point $(x,y)$ would like a slope of $y/x$. The best single slope is a weighted average of those wishes, where points with larger $x$ get more say.
cards.definition:
$$w=\frac{\sum xy}{\sum x^2}$$

Symbols: $\sum xy$ means "multiply each $x$ by its $y$, then add all the products". $\sum x^2$ means "square each $x$, then add". The formula comes from minimising $\sum (y-wx)^2$. Its slope in $w$ is $-2\sum x(y-wx)$, and setting that to zero gives $w$.
cards.intuition_full: Write the SSE as a function of $w$: $\sum (y-wx)^2$. Expanding the bracket gives $w^2\sum x^2-2w\sum xy+\sum y^2$. This is a bowl-shaped curve (a parabola) in $w$, and its lowest point is at $w=\sum xy/\sum x^2$. It is the school rule "the bottom of $ax^2+bx+c$ is at $-b/2a$" with $a=\sum x^2$ and $b=-2\sum xy$. Another way to see it: a point with a big $x$ pins the line strongly, because a small change in $w$ moves the prediction a lot there. Its wish $y/x$ is therefore weighted by $x^2$. A point at $x=0$ says nothing about the slope, and the formula agrees, since it adds 0 to both sums.

cards.title: Slope and intercept
cards.simple: Now let the ruler slide as well as swing. Here is a neat fact: the best ruler always passes through the "average dot", whose x is the average of all the x values and whose y is the average of all the y values. So pin the ruler there and swing it. The steepness depends on whether dots that are further right than average also tend to be higher than average. Once you know the steepness, you can read off where the ruler crosses the y-axis. In exam words: slope $w=S_{xy}/S_{xx}$ and intercept $b=\bar y-w\bar x$.
cards.idea: Now the line may sit anywhere: $\hat y=wx+b$. The best line always passes through the **average point** $(\bar x,\bar y)$, so find that first. Then ask how $x$ and $y$ move together around it. If dots right of the average tend to be above the average, the slope is positive. The intercept $b$ then says where the line crosses $x=0$.
cards.definition:
$$w=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}},\qquad b=\bar y-w\,\bar x$$

where $S_{xy}=\sum (x-\bar x)(y-\bar y)$ and $S_{xx}=\sum (x-\bar x)^2$.

Symbols: $\bar x$ is the mean of the $x$ values and $\bar y$ the mean of the $y$ values. $(x-\bar x)$ is how far a point sits from the average in $x$, and $(y-\bar y)$ is the same in $y$. $S_{xy}$ adds the products of those two distances. $S_{xx}$ adds the squared $x$ distances.

Shortcut when you only have totals: $S_{xy}=\sum xy-n\bar x\bar y$ and $S_{xx}=\sum x^2-n\bar x^2$.
cards.intuition_full: Split the plane into four quarters around the average point. A dot in the top-right or bottom-left quarter has two distances of the same sign, so its product is positive and it pulls the slope up. A dot in the top-left or bottom-right has opposite signs, so its product is negative and it pulls the slope down. $S_{xy}$ is the total pull, drawn as signed rectangle areas in the animation. Dividing by $S_{xx}$ turns the pull into "change in $y$ per change in $x$". Why must the line pass through $(\bar x,\bar y)$? If it did not, you could slide the whole line up or down until its residuals average to zero, and that always lowers the SSE. So the best intercept is $b=\bar y-w\bar x$, which is the same as saying the line goes through the mean point.

examples.setup: Using the four points from the basic example, a student regresses $x$ on $y$ and then inverts the slope to get the slope of $y$ on $x$. Does that work?
steps: Regress $x$ on $y$: the slope is $S_{xy}/S_{yy}$. Here $S_{yy}=2.25+0.25+0.25+6.25=9$.
That slope is $6/9=0.667$. Inverting it gives $1/0.667=1.5$.
The true slope of $y$ on $x$ is $6/5=1.2$. So $1.5\ne1.2$.
The two slopes multiply to $0.667\cdot1.2=0.8$, which is $r^2$. They are inverses of each other only when the points are perfectly collinear ($r^2=1$).
examples.answer: No. Regression of $y$ on $x$ and of $x$ on $y$ give different lines. Their slopes multiply to $r^2$, not to 1.

cards.why: These two formulas are what GATE means by "fit a line by hand". The same centred sums come back in R-squared and in correlation. In GATE: summary totals or three to four points, and you find the slope, the intercept or a prediction.
how: Find $\bar x$ and $\bar y$.
Compute $S_{xy}$ and $S_{xx}$, from distances or from $\sum xy-n\bar x\bar y$ and $\sum x^2-n\bar x^2$.
Slope $w=S_{xy}/S_{xx}$.
Intercept $b=\bar y-w\bar x$. Check that the line passes through $(\bar x,\bar y)$.
cards.mistake: Stopping after the slope, or using $\sum xy/\sum x^2$ because it is shorter. That formula is for the no-intercept model. With an intercept, centre the data first, then find $b$ from the means.
edge_cases: If all $x$ values are equal, $S_{xx}=0$ and there is no unique line (it would be vertical).
If $S_{xy}=0$ the slope is 0 and the best line is flat at $\bar y$.
Adding the same number to every $x$ changes the intercept but not the slope.
With only two points the line passes exactly through both and SSE is 0.
connections: Foundations: Algebra. Averaging and rearranging $b=\bar y-w\bar x$ is plain algebra.
Residual properties (the next card): the mean-point fact is why residuals sum to 0.
Descriptive statistics and moments: $S_{xx}/n$ is the variance and $S_{xy}/n$ is the covariance.

**Worked example.** Fit $\hat y=wx+b$ to (1,1), (2,2), (3,2), (4,5).

1. Means: $\bar x=(1+2+3+4)/4=2.5$ and $\bar y=(1+2+2+5)/4=2.5$.
2. Distances from the means. For $x$: $-1.5,\ -0.5,\ 0.5,\ 1.5$. For $y$: $-1.5,\ -0.5,\ -0.5,\ 2.5$.
3. Products: $2.25,\ 0.25,\ -0.25,\ 3.75$. So $S_{xy}=2.25+0.25-0.25+3.75=6$.
4. Squared $x$ distances: $2.25,\ 0.25,\ 0.25,\ 2.25$. So $S_{xx}=5$.
5. Slope $w=6/5=1.2$. Intercept $b=2.5-1.2\cdot2.5=2.5-3=-0.5$.
6. Check: at $x=2.5$ the line gives $1.2\cdot2.5-0.5=2.5$, so it passes through the mean point.

**Answer:** $\hat y=1.2x-0.5$.

**Check yourself:** The means are $\bar x=3$ and $\bar y=7$, with $S_{xy}=10$ and $S_{xx}=5$. Find $w$ and $b$.

*Answer:* $w=10/5=2$. $b=7-2\cdot3=1$.

cards.title: Residual properties
cards.simple: After you place the best sliding ruler, the dots above it and the dots below it balance out, like a see-saw. Add up how far the dots above sit, add up how far the dots below sit, and the two totals are equal. So all the signed misses together come to zero. That is handy: if every miss but one is known, you can get the last one without fitting anything. It only works when the ruler was allowed to slide up and down, which means the line has an intercept. In exam words: with an intercept the residuals sum to zero, $\sum e=0$, and also $\sum e\,x=0$.
cards.idea: For the best line with an intercept, the misses balance. The residuals above the line add up to the same size as the residuals below it, so $\sum e=0$. They also balance when each is weighted by its $x$: $\sum e\,x=0$. These are two quick facts you can use to check a hand fit or to find a missing residual.
cards.definition:
$$\sum_i e_i=0,\qquad \sum_i e_i\,x_i=0$$

Both hold for the least-squares line when the model has an intercept. Symbols: $e_i$ is the residual of point $i$ and $x_i$ is its $x$ value.

They come from the normal equations: the list of residuals is perpendicular to the column of ones (giving $\sum e=0$) and to the column of $x$ values (giving $\sum ex=0$). Without an intercept the ones column is not in the model, so only $\sum ex=0$ is guaranteed.
cards.intuition_full: Think of the line as a see-saw. If the residuals added to a positive number, the dots would sit above the line on average, and sliding the line up would lower the SSE. So at the best line, sliding up or down cannot help, which means the sum is 0. In the same way, if the residuals weighted by $x$ did not cancel, tilting the line a little would lower the SSE. The best line is exactly the line where neither a slide nor a tilt helps. Each condition is one equation, and a line has two parameters ($w$ and $b$), so you get two equations: $\sum e=0$ and $\sum ex=0$. These are the normal equations in disguise.

example.setup: Use the fitted line $\hat y=1.2x-0.5$ for the points (1,1), (2,2), (3,2), (4,5).
steps: Below the line: $-1.1$. The two sides have the same size.
example.answer: Both sums are 0, which confirms the line is the least-squares fit.

examples.setup: A line with intercept is fitted by least squares to 6 points at $x=1,2,3,4,5,6$. The first four residuals are $1,\ -2,\ 0,\ 1$. Find the last two, $e_5$ and $e_6$.

examples.answer: $\sum e\ne0$ but $\sum ex=0$. Without an intercept the ones column is not in the model, so only the $x$-column condition survives.

cards.why: These identities turn a long fit into a short sum, and they are the easiest way to check a hand fit. In GATE: a property statement such as "the residuals always sum to zero", or a missing residual to find.

Add the known residuals. The missing one is minus that sum.
If two residuals are missing, also use $\sum e\,x=0$ and solve two equations.
To verify a hand fit, check that both sums come out 0.
cards.mistake: Applying $\sum e=0$ to a model without an intercept, or to a line that is not the least-squares line. The residuals of an arbitrary line need not sum to zero.
edge_cases: Residuals summing to 0 does not prove the line is good. The line $\hat y=x$ in the first card had signed sum 0 and a worse SSE.
If all residuals are 0, both sums are 0 trivially (the points lie on a line).
The mean residual is 0, so the mean of $\hat y$ equals the mean of $y$.
One feature gives exactly 2 constraints, so you can recover at most 2 missing residuals.
connections: Normal equations (a later card): these two sums are those equations written for one feature.
Linear Algebra: Projection, orthogonality and quadratic forms. The residual list is perpendicular to the ones column and to the $x$ column.
R-squared: because $\sum e=0$, the fit has the same mean as $y$, which is why the SST split works.

check.q: A least-squares line with intercept has residuals 3, −1 and $e$. What is $e$?
Does $\sum e=0$ always hold for a through-origin fit?
check.a: No. Only $\sum ex=0$ is guaranteed there.

check.q: Residuals at $x=1,2,3$ are $a,\ b,\ c$ with $a+b+c=0$ and $a+2b+3c=0$. What is the ratio $a:b:c$?
check.a: Subtract the first equation from the second: $b+2c=0$, so $b=-2c$. Then $a=-b-c=c$. The ratio is $1:-2:1$.

cards.title: R-squared
cards.simple: Suppose you must guess every student's marks. The lazy guess is to give everybody the class average. The mistakes of that lazy guess add up to one big number. Now guess using the best line instead, and its mistakes add up to a smaller number. R-squared says what fraction of the lazy guess's mistakes the line got rid of. If the lazy guess made 9 units of mistakes and the line made 1.8, the line removed 80 percent, so R-squared is 0.8. In exam words: $R^2=1-\text{SSE}/\text{SST}$.
cards.idea: How good is the line? Compare it with the laziest possible guess, which is to predict the average $\bar y$ for every point. That lazy guess has its own total squared error, called **SST**. Your line has a smaller error, **SSE**. R-squared is the fraction of SST that the line removed. A value of 1 is a perfect fit, and 0 means no better than the average.
cards.definition:
$$R^2=1-\frac{\text{SSE}}{\text{SST}},\qquad \text{SST}=\sum (y-\bar y)^2$$

Symbols: SST is the "total variation" in $y$, which is the SSE of the flat line at $\bar y$. SSE is the squared error of your fitted line. The fraction $\text{SSE}/\text{SST}$ is the share you failed to explain.

For one feature with an intercept, $R^2=r^2$, where $r$ is the correlation between $x$ and $y$.
cards.intuition_full: For a least-squares line with an intercept, the total variation splits cleanly: SST = SSE + SSR, where SSR is the part the line explains. Dividing by SST turns these into shares that add to 1, and R-squared is the explained share. The lazy guess is one of the lines least squares could have picked (slope 0), so the best line can never do worse on the training data. That is why training R-squared lies between 0 and 1. Think of marks again. If students vary a lot (large SST) but the line predicts each within a mark or two (small SSE), you have explained nearly all the spread. R-squared says nothing about whether the line has the right shape, or how it does on new data. It only measures how much of the training spread the line absorbed.

example.setup: Points (1,1), (2,2), (3,2), (4,5). Their least-squares line is $\hat y=1.2x-0.5$. Find $R^2$.
steps: The lazy guess is $\bar y=2.5$. Its misses are $-1.5,\ -0.5,\ -0.5,\ +2.5$.
The line's residuals are $0.3,\ 0.1,\ -1.1,\ 0.7$, so the line is far closer to the dots.
$R^2=1-0.2=0.8$. The line explains 80 percent of the ups and downs in $y$.

examples.setup: Points (1,1), (2,2), (3,2), (4,5). Their least-squares line is $\hat y=1.2x-0.5$. Find $R^2$.

examples.setup: On new data, $y=(2,4,6)$ and a model predicts $\hat y=(6,4,2)$. Find $R^2$.
examples.answer: $R^2=-3$. R-squared can be negative when a model is worse than predicting the mean. A least-squares fit with an intercept cannot do this on its own training data, but a model can on new data.

edge_cases: $R^2=1$ means every point sits exactly on the line (SSE = 0).

cards.title: Rescaling and shifting
cards.simple: A slope says how much y changes for each step of x. If you count x in smaller steps, each step moves y less, so the slope number gets smaller. Think of a taxi that charges 10 rupees per km. Count distance in metres instead, and the price per metre is only 0.01 rupees. The line on the graph is the same line, and only the numbers on the x-axis changed. If you add 5 marks to everyone, the whole line just slides up by 5. In exam words: scale $x$ by $c$ and the slope divides by $c$; shift $y$ by $d$ and the intercept moves by $d$.
cards.idea: A fitted line is a statement such as "4 more marks for each extra hour". If you change the units, the line does not change, but the numbers do. Count $x$ in half-hours and each step is smaller, so the slope per step is smaller. Slide all the $y$ values up and the line slides up, so only the intercept changes. These unit changes are quick marks if you remember which way each number moves.
cards.definition:
Let the fitted line be $\hat y=wx+b$.

- **Scale $x$:** with $x'=cx$, the new slope is $w'=w/c$ and the intercept stays $b$.
- **Scale $y$:** with $y'=ky$, both numbers scale: $w'=kw$ and $b'=kb$.
- **Shift $y$:** with $y'=y+d$, the slope stays and $b'=b+d$.
- **Shift $x$:** with $x'=x+d$, the slope stays and $b'=b-wd$.

Symbols: $c$ and $k$ are positive scale factors and $d$ is a shift. Method: write the old variable in terms of the new one, substitute into $\hat y=wx+b$, and collect terms.
cards.intuition_full: The data is the same. You are only changing the ruler along each axis. If $x$ is stretched by $c$, the dots spread out sideways by $c$, so the best line gets flatter by the same factor, giving slope $w/c$. Its height at $x'=0$ has not changed, so the intercept stays. If $y$ is stretched by $k$, everything on the vertical scale grows by $k$, including the height where the line crosses the y-axis. A shift of $y$ slides all dots up, so it slides the line up by the same amount. Shifting $x$ slides the dots sideways, so the line crosses $x'=0$ at a different height, and that is why the intercept changes by $-wd$. A useful special case: shift $x$ by $-\bar x$ (centre it), and the intercept becomes $\bar y$.

example.setup: Hours studied $x$ and marks $y$: (1,2), (2,3), (3,4), (4,5). The fitted line is $\hat y=x+1$ (slope 1, intercept 1). Now count time in half-hours, $x'=2x$, and then add 2 marks to every $y$.
steps: Original fit: $w=1$ and $b=1$. At 3 hours the line gives $3+1=4$ marks.
Count in half-hours: $x'=2x$, so the points become (2,2), (4,3), (6,4), (8,5). The same data, spread twice as wide. The old line no longer fits them.
New fit: the slope is $1/2=0.5$ and the intercept is still 1. At $x'=6$ (3 hours) it gives $0.5\cdot6+1=4$ marks, the same as before.
Add 2 to every $y$: the points become (2,4), (4,5), (6,6), (8,7). The line slides up 2 and becomes $\hat y=0.5x'+3$.
Rule: scaling $x$ by $c$ divides the slope by $c$. Shifting $y$ by $d$ adds $d$ to the intercept.

examples.setup: Hours studied $x$ and marks $y$: (1,2), (2,3), (3,4), (4,5). The fitted line is $\hat y=x+1$ (slope 1, intercept 1). Now count time in half-hours, $x'=2x$, and then add 2 marks to every $y$.

examples.setup: A model for house price in thousands of rupees against distance in km is $\hat y=0.6x+12$. The data is re-recorded with price in rupees ($y'=1000y$) and distance in metres ($x'=1000x$). Find the new slope and intercept.
steps: Write the old variables with the new ones: $x=x'/1000$ and $y=y'/1000$.
Slope: the two scale factors cancel, $0.6\cdot\tfrac{1000}{1000}=0.6$. Intercept: $12\cdot1000=12000$.
examples.answer: New slope $0.6$ and new intercept $12000$. In general the slope is multiplied by $k/c$ and the intercept by $k$.

examples.setup: The fitted line is $\hat y=2x+3$ and $\bar x=4$. Shift $x$ to $x'=x-4$ (centre it). What are the new slope and intercept?
steps: The slope is still 2 and the intercept is $11$.
Check: at the mean $x=4$ the old line gives $2\cdot4+3=11$, which is $\bar y$ because the line passes through the mean point.
examples.answer: Slope 2, intercept 11, which equals $\bar y$. Centring $x$ makes the intercept the mean of $y$.

Write the old variable in terms of the new one and substitute into $\hat y=wx+b$.
Collect terms: the coefficient of the new $x$ is the slope, the constant is the intercept.
Check one point: the prediction must be the same after converting back.
cards.mistake: Multiplying the slope when $x$ is scaled up. If you measure $x$ in smaller units, its numbers get bigger, each unit buys less, and the slope shrinks. Substitute and rewrite instead of guessing the direction.
edge_cases: Scaling $x$ by a negative $c$ flips the sign of the slope.

$R^2$ and the correlation do not change under positive scaling or shifting of either variable.

1. Original fit: $w=1$ and $b=1$. At 3 hours the line gives $3+1=4$ marks.
2. Count in half-hours: $x'=2x$, so the points become (2,2), (4,3), (6,4), (8,5). The same data, spread twice as wide. The old line no longer fits them.
3. New fit: the slope is $1/2=0.5$ and the intercept is still 1. At $x'=6$ (3 hours) it gives $0.5\cdot6+1=4$ marks, the same as before.
4. Add 2 to every $y$: the points become (2,4), (4,5), (6,6), (8,7). The line slides up 2 and becomes $\hat y=0.5x'+3$.
5. Rule: scaling $x$ by $c$ divides the slope by $c$. Shifting $y$ by $d$ adds $d$ to the intercept.

**Answer:** After $x'=2x$: $\hat y=0.5x'+1$. After also $y'=y+2$: $\hat y'=0.5x'+3$.

**Check yourself:** A line has slope 3 per km. What is the slope per metre?

*Answer:* One metre is $1/1000$ of a km, so the slope is $3/1000=0.003$.

cards.title: Normal equations
cards.simple: Imagine the true answers as an arrow pointing somewhere in space, and everything your model can possibly predict as a flat table top in that space. The best prediction is the shadow of the arrow on the table, straight down. The leftover piece, from the shadow up to the arrow, stands at a right angle to the table. That right-angle rule is the whole trick. Write it as an equation and you get the normal equations, which work for any number of features. In exam words: the least-squares weights satisfy $X^\top X\,w=X^\top y$.
cards.idea: With many features you cannot work with plain sums of $x$ and $y$. The normal equations are one matrix equation that covers every case: $X^\top X\,w=X^\top y$. The picture behind them is simple. The model's predictions $Xw$ can only lie on a flat sheet, made of all combinations of the columns of $X$. The best prediction is the point on that sheet closest to $y$, which is the foot of the perpendicular. So the leftover residual is at right angles to every column.
cards.definition:
$$X^\top X\,w=X^\top y\quad\Longrightarrow\quad w=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y$$

Symbols: $X$ is the data matrix with one row per sample and one column per feature, plus a column of ones for the intercept. $y$ is the vector of targets. $w$ is the vector of weights. $X^\top$ is $X$ with rows and columns swapped.

The equation says $X^\top(y-Xw)=0$: the residual $y-Xw$ has dot product 0 with every column of $X$. The inverse exists only when the columns of $X$ are independent.
cards.intuition_full: Write SSE $=\|y-Xw\|^2$. Its gradient is $-2X^\top(y-Xw)$. Setting that to zero says every column of $X$ is perpendicular to the residual, which is the "shadow" picture. For a single column $x$ with no intercept, the equation reads $(x\cdot x)\,w=x\cdot y$, which is $w=\sum xy/\sum x^2$, the formula you already know. With a column of ones as well, the first equation says $\sum e=0$ and the second says $\sum ex=0$, the two residual properties. So the normal equations are the same facts in matrix form, valid for any number of features. $X^\top X$ collects the dot products of every pair of columns, and $X^\top y$ collects the dot product of each column with $y$.

example.setup: Two samples and one feature, no intercept. The feature column is $x=(3,1)$ and the targets are $y=(1,3)$. Model: $\hat y=wx$. Solve the normal equation and check the right angle.
example.answer: $w=0.6$. The residual is perpendicular to the column, as the normal equations require.

examples.setup: Two samples and one feature, no intercept. The feature column is $x=(3,1)$ and the targets are $y=(1,3)$. Model: $\hat y=wx$. Solve the normal equation and check the right angle.

examples.setup: Samples $(x,y)$: (0,2), (1,3), (2,7). Fit $\hat y=b+wx$ using the normal equations, and say how many parameters the model has.
steps: Design matrix with a ones column: rows $(1,0),\ (1,1),\ (1,2)$. Parameters: $b$ and $w$, so 2 (one feature plus one intercept).
The equations are $3b+3w=12$ and $3b+5w=17$. Subtract the first from the second: $2w=5$, so $w=2.5$.
Then $3b+7.5=12$, so $b=1.5$. The residuals are $2-1.5=0.5$, $3-4=-1$, $7-6.5=0.5$, which sum to 0 as expected.
examples.answer: $\hat y=1.5+2.5x$, with 2 parameters.

examples.setup: Two samples and two **identical** feature columns $(1,2)$ and $(1,2)$, with targets $y=(3,6)$. Solve $X^\top Xw=X^\top y$.
steps: $X^\top X=\begin{pmatrix}5&5\\5&5\end{pmatrix}$. Its determinant is $25-25=0$, so there is no inverse.
Both equations say $5w_1+5w_2=15$, which is $w_1+w_2=3$. There are infinitely many solutions, such as $(3,0)$ and $(1.5,1.5)$.
examples.answer: The equation $X^\top Xw=X^\top y$ still has solutions, but not a unique one, and the formula with the inverse breaks. The fitted values $(3,6)$ are unique.

how: Build $X$ with a column of ones if the model has an intercept.
Compute $X^\top X$ (dot products of the columns) and $X^\top y$.
Solve the small system $X^\top X\,w=X^\top y$ by elimination.
Check: the residual $y-Xw$ should be perpendicular to every column.
cards.mistake: Writing $XX^\top$ instead of $X^\top X$, or forgetting the column of ones. $X^\top X$ has size (features + 1) by (features + 1), while $XX^\top$ has size samples by samples.
edge_cases: One column and no intercept: the equation collapses to $w=\sum xy/\sum x^2$.
Duplicate or dependent columns: $X^\top X$ has no inverse, but the equation still has solutions.
Fewer samples than parameters: infinitely many exact fits, and $X^\top X$ is singular.
A perfect fit means the residual is the zero vector, so $y$ lies in the column space.
connections: Linear Algebra: Systems of equations and rank. Rank decides when the solution is unique.

Foundations: Derivatives. Setting the gradient of SSE to zero produces the equation.

check.a: The residual vector has dot product 0 with every column of $X$. It is perpendicular to all of them.

cards.title: Parameters and invertibility
cards.simple: A straight line has two settings: how steep it is, and how high it sits. To fix two settings you need two clues. One dot is only one clue, so many lines pass through it. Two dots at different positions along the x-axis pin the line down. But two dots stacked straight above each other give you only one clue about height and none about steepness, so many lines fit equally well. This card is about counting the settings and checking that your clues are independent. In exam words: $d$ features plus an intercept means $d+1$ weights, and the solution is unique only if $X$ has full column rank.
cards.idea: A model with $d$ features and an intercept has $d+1$ weights to learn. A line ($d=1$) has 2, the slope and the intercept. To pin down all of them, the data must give $d+1$ independent clues. If two columns of the data say the same thing (one is a copy or a multiple of another), the weights cannot be told apart. The fitted predictions are still fine, but the individual weights are not unique.
cards.definition:
- Number of weights: $d+1$ ($d$ features plus 1 intercept).
- $X^\top X$ is a $(d+1)\times(d+1)$ matrix.
- $X^\top X$ is invertible **if and only if** the columns of $X$ are linearly independent (full column rank). That needs at least $d+1$ samples and no column that is a combination of the others.
- If it is not invertible, infinitely many weight vectors give the same minimum SSE, and they all give the same predictions $Xw$.

Symbols: $d$ is the number of input features, $n$ the number of samples, and $X$ the $n\times(d+1)$ data matrix with a ones column.
cards.intuition_full: Think of equations and unknowns. The normal equations are $d+1$ equations in $d+1$ unknowns, but they only help if none of them repeats another. A duplicated column makes two equations the same, so you lose one equation and gain a free choice: shift weight from one copy to the other and nothing changes. Geometrically, the sheet of possible predictions (the column space) does not get any bigger when you add a column that already lies in it. So the shadow of $y$ on it is the same. The shadow, meaning the predictions, is unique. The recipe for building it from the columns is not. Too few samples cause the same problem: with fewer rows than columns the columns cannot be independent, so some combination of weights does nothing.

example.setup: A line $\hat y=wx+b$ has 2 weights. See how many lines the data allows with one point, with two points at different $x$, and with two points at the same $x$.
steps: Count: one feature plus an intercept gives $d+1=2$ weights, $w$ and $b$.
One point $(2,3)$: many lines fit it exactly, for example $\hat y=3$, $\hat y=x+1$ and $\hat y=2x-1$. One clue cannot fix two weights.

Two points $(1,2)$ and $(3,5)$ with different $x$: slope $(5-2)/(3-1)=1.5$, then $b=2-1.5\cdot1=0.5$. One line only. Here $X^\top X=\begin{pmatrix}2&4\\4&10\end{pmatrix}$ with determinant $20-16=4\ne0$.
Two points $(2,1)$ and $(2,3)$ with the same $x$: $X^\top X=\begin{pmatrix}2&4\\4&8\end{pmatrix}$ with determinant $16-16=0$. It is singular. Every line through $(2,2)$ has the same SSE of 2.
At $x=2$ every one of those lines predicts 2. The weights are not unique, but the prediction is.
example.answer: Two weights need two independent clues. Different $x$ values give a unique line (determinant 4). The same $x$ twice gives a singular $X^\top X$ (determinant 0) and infinitely many lines, but only one prediction at $x=2$.

examples.setup: A regression uses a ones column and two features, where the second is always twice the first ($x_2=2x_1$). The data: $x_1=1,2,3,4$ and $y=2,3,5,6$. (a) Is $X^\top X$ invertible? (b) What do the fit and $w_1+2w_2$ equal? (c) What is the prediction at $x_1=5$ (so $x_2=10$)?
steps: The columns are $(1,1,1,1)$, $(1,2,3,4)$ and $(2,4,6,8)$. The third is twice the second, so the rank is 2, not 3. $X^\top X$ is $3\times3$ and singular. The model still has 3 parameters.
Fit $y$ on $x_1$ alone: $\bar x=2.5$, $\bar y=4$, $S_{xy}=7$, $S_{xx}=5$. The slope is $1.4$ and the intercept is $4-1.4\cdot2.5=0.5$.
With the copy, the model is $\hat y=b+w_1x_1+w_2(2x_1)=b+(w_1+2w_2)x_1$. Only the combination $w_1+2w_2=1.4$ is fixed, and $b=0.5$.
Prediction at $x_1=5$: $0.5+1.4\cdot5=7.5$, whichever pair you pick.
examples.answer: (a) No, $X^\top X$ is singular. (b) $b=0.5$ and $w_1+2w_2=1.4$, with many solutions. (c) 7.5. The weights are not unique, the predictions are.

examples.setup: Three weights (a ones column, $x_1$ and $x_2$) but only two samples: rows $(1,1,0)$ and $(1,0,1)$. No column is a copy of another. Is $X^\top X$ invertible?
steps: It is singular. The rank of $X$ is at most the number of rows, 2, which is less than the 3 columns.
Three unknowns with two equations: infinitely many weight vectors fit both samples exactly.
examples.answer: Not invertible. Fewer samples than weights makes $X^\top X$ singular even when no two columns look alike. You need $n\ge d+1$ and independent columns.

cards.why: Counting weights is a free mark, and "when are the weights unique?" is the follow-up. This is where regression meets rank from linear algebra, and it is exactly why ridge regression adds $\lambda I$. In GATE: "how many weights?", "is $X^\top X$ invertible?", or "a column is duplicated: what is true?".
how: Count the weights: features plus 1 for the intercept.
Check the columns: is any column a copy or multiple of the others? Are there fewer samples than weights?
If yes: $X^\top X$ is singular, the weights are not unique, and the predictions $Xw$ are unique.
If no: $w=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y$ is the unique solution.
cards.mistake: Saying the predictions are non-unique when columns are duplicated. Only the weights are non-unique. The fitted values and the minimum SSE are the same for every solution.
edge_cases: Exactly $d+1$ independent samples: the model passes through every point (SSE = 0).
A constant feature column duplicates the ones column, so it is collinear with the intercept.
Nearly duplicated columns give an invertible but unstable $X^\top X$. Tiny changes in the data move the weights a lot.
Rank needs $n\ge d+1$, but having $n\ge d+1$ does not by itself guarantee independent columns.
connections: Linear Algebra: Systems of equations and rank. A unique solution means full column rank.
Ridge regression: $X^\top X+\lambda I$ is invertible for every $\lambda>0$, which cures collinearity.
Normal equations (the previous card): the equation always has a solution, the inverse formula needs full rank.

check.q: A model has 5 features and an intercept. How many weights?
$n=4$ samples, $d=5$ features plus an intercept. Can $X^\top X$ be invertible?
check.a: No. There are 6 columns but only 4 rows, so the rank is at most 4.

check.q: Two features are identical. Are the fitted values unique?
check.a: Yes. Only the split of weight between the two copies is free.

cards.title: Adding more features
cards.simple: Adding a new column of information to a model is like giving yourself one more dial to turn. With an extra dial you can always set it to zero and get your old answer back, so you can never do worse on the data you are tuning on. The training score can only stay the same or get better. But that does not make the model better in real life. With enough dials you can fit noise, like memorising last year's question paper instead of learning the subject. In exam words: adding a feature never increases the training SSE, but it can increase the test error.
cards.idea: Add a column to $X$ and the model gets one more weight to set. Setting that weight to 0 gives back the old model, so the new best fit is at least as good as the old one. So training SSE never goes up when you add a feature. It does not follow that predictions on new data get better. A feature that is only noise can still lower the training SSE and make the test error worse.
cards.definition:
Let $\text{SSE}_A$ be the best training SSE with feature set $A$, and let $B$ be $A$ plus one more feature $z$. Then

$$\text{SSE}_B\le\text{SSE}_A,\qquad R^2_B\ge R^2_A$$

Symbols: $z$ is the extra column. Reason: the weight vector for $B$ with weight 0 on $z$ is one of the choices, and it reproduces fit $A$ exactly. Least squares picks the best of all choices, so it can only match or beat $A$. With $n$ samples and $n$ independent columns the fit passes through every point (SSE = 0).
cards.intuition_full: Think of a tailor. With two measurements he can make a coat that fits you roughly. Give him a third measurement and he can do the same or better, because he can ignore the new number. His skill on the person standing in front of him can only improve. But if the third measurement is meaningless (say, what you had for lunch), he may start fitting the coat to the lunch, and the coat will fit worse on another day. Training error is measured on the data used to set the weights, so it always rewards extra freedom. Test error is measured on fresh data, so it also punishes fitting noise. That gap between the two is overfitting, the subject of bias and variance.

example.setup: Points (1,2), (2,1), (3,4), (4,3). Compare three models: only an intercept; then intercept plus $x$; then intercept plus $x$ plus a flag $z=(1,0,1,0)$.
steps: Intercept only: predict $\bar y=2.5$ everywhere. Residuals $-0.5,\ -1.5,\ 1.5,\ 0.5$, so SSE $=0.25+2.25+2.25+0.25=5$.
Add the flag $z$ (1 for points 1 and 3): the fit is $\hat y=-1+x+2z$. Predictions $2,\ 1,\ 4,\ 3$ match every $y$, so SSE $=0$.
SSE went $5\to3.2\to0$. It never rose. Setting a new weight to 0 would give back the previous model, so the best fit can only match or beat it.
example.answer: SSE falls $5\to3.2\to0$ and $R^2$ rises $0\to0.36\to1$. Each added column could only help the training fit.

examples.setup: Model A uses feature $x_1$ and has training SSE $=12.5$ with SST $=50$. Model B adds a second feature $x_2$ and is refitted. Which values are possible for Model B: (i) SSE $=12.5$, (ii) SSE $=14$, (iii) SSE $=9$, (iv) $R^2=0.74$?
steps: B can ignore $x_2$ (weight 0), so B's best SSE is at most 12.5: $\text{SSE}_B\le12.5$.
(i) 12.5 is possible if $x_2$ is useless. (ii) 14 is impossible, since it is above 12.5. (iii) 9 is possible.
(iv) $R^2=0.74$ would mean SSE $=50(1-0.74)=13$, which is above 12.5, so it is impossible. $R^2_B\ge0.75$.
examples.answer: Possible: (i) and (iii). Impossible: (ii) and (iv). Training SSE can only stay or fall, and training $R^2$ can only stay or rise.

examples.setup: Use the data of the basic example. Suppose the true relationship is a straight line in $x$ plus noise, and $z$ is just a noisy flag. A new point arrives with $x=5$, $z=1$ and true $y\approx4.2$. Compare the model with $x$ and the model with $x$ and $z$.
steps: The bigger model fitted the noise in the flag. It does worse on new data despite SSE $=0$ on the training data.
examples.answer: Training SSE fell from 3.2 to 0, but the squared error on the new point rose from 0.04 to 3.24. More features can overfit.

cards.why: The fact that "training error always falls when you add a feature" is one of the most reliable multiple-select statements, and it is the doorway to overfitting. In GATE: a statement about SSE, $R^2$ or test error after adding a feature.
how: Compare the models: B has all of A's features plus more.
Training SSE: B is less than or equal to A. Training $R^2$: B is greater than or equal to A.
Test error: there is no guarantee in either direction. Never claim it falls.
If a number is given, check it does not break $\text{SSE}_B\le\text{SSE}_A$.
cards.mistake: Saying "more features always gives a better model". It only guarantees a better training fit. On new data, extra noisy features raise the variance of the predictions.
edge_cases: A useless feature may leave SSE exactly unchanged (equal, not strictly less).
With $n$ independent columns for $n$ samples, SSE reaches 0.
A duplicate of an existing column never changes SSE.
Held-out error usually falls at first and then rises as useless features pile in.
connections: Bias and variance: the extra freedom lowers bias on the training set and raises variance.
Cross-validation is the tool for checking whether an added feature really helps.
R-squared (an earlier card): training $R^2$ never falls when a column is added.

check.q: SSE with one feature is 8. A second feature is added. Can the new SSE be 8.5?
check.a: No. It can be 8 or smaller.

check.q: Does adding a feature always reduce the test error?
check.a: No. It only guarantees that the training SSE does not rise.

check.q: A model has $R^2=0.6$. A copy of one existing column is added. What is the new $R^2$?
check.a: Still 0.6. A copy adds no new information.

try.label: Effect of adding a feature on training SSE

cards.what: Add a column to $X$ and the model gets one more weight to set. Setting that weight to 0 gives back the old model, so the new best fit is at least as good as the old one. So training SSE never goes up when you add a feature. It does not follow that predictions on new data get better. A feature that is only noise can still lower the training SSE and make the test error worse.
cards.what_full:
Add a column to $X$ and the model gets one more weight to set. Setting that weight to 0 gives back the old model, so the new best fit is at least as good as the old one. So training SSE never goes up when you add a feature. It does not follow that predictions on new data get better. A feature that is only noise can still lower the training SSE and make the test error worse.

Let $\text{SSE}_A$ be the best training SSE with feature set $A$, and let $B$ be $A$ plus one more feature $z$. Then

$$\text{SSE}_B\le\text{SSE}_A,\qquad R^2_B\ge R^2_A$$

Symbols: $z$ is the extra column. Reason: the weight vector for $B$ with weight 0 on $z$ is one of the choices, and it reproduces fit $A$ exactly. Least squares picks the best of all choices, so it can only match or beat $A$. With $n$ samples and $n$ independent columns the fit passes through every point (SSE = 0).

**Worked example.** Points (1,2), (2,1), (3,4), (4,3). Compare three models: only an intercept; then intercept plus $x$; then intercept plus $x$ plus a flag $z=(1,0,1,0)$.

1. Intercept only: predict $\bar y=2.5$ everywhere. Residuals $-0.5,\ -1.5,\ 1.5,\ 0.5$, so SSE $=0.25+2.25+2.25+0.25=5$.
2. Add $x$: the fit is $\hat y=0.6x+1$. Predictions $1.6,\ 2.2,\ 2.8,\ 3.4$ give residuals $0.4,\ -1.2,\ 1.2,\ -0.4$, so SSE $=0.16+1.44+1.44+0.16=3.2$.
3. Add the flag $z$ (1 for points 1 and 3): the fit is $\hat y=-1+x+2z$. Predictions $2,\ 1,\ 4,\ 3$ match every $y$, so SSE $=0$.
4. SSE went $5\to3.2\to0$. It never rose. Setting a new weight to 0 would give back the previous model, so the best fit can only match or beat it.

**Answer:** SSE falls $5\to3.2\to0$ and $R^2$ rises $0\to0.36\to1$. Each added column could only help the training fit.

**Check yourself:** SSE with one feature is 8. A second feature is added. Can the new SSE be 8.5?

*Answer:* No. It can be 8 or smaller.

cards.title: Gradient step
cards.simple: Imagine you are standing on a hillside in fog and you want to reach the valley. You cannot see the valley, but you can feel which way the ground slopes under your feet. So you take a small step downhill, feel the slope again, and repeat. The height of the ground is the loss, and where you stand is the weight. A steep slope gives a big step, a flat slope gives a tiny step, and you stop at the bottom. In exam words: $w\leftarrow w-\eta\,\partial L/\partial w$, and for squared loss the gradient is $(wx-y)x$.
cards.idea: Gradient descent finds the best weight by repeated small downhill steps. At the current weight, work out how the loss changes when you nudge $w$. That rate of change is the **gradient**. Then move $w$ a small step against it. The step size is set by the learning rate $\eta$. For squared error the gradient has a simple form: the error times the input.
cards.definition:
For one sample with loss $L=\tfrac12(wx-y)^2$:

$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial w}=(wx-y)\,x,\qquad w\leftarrow w-\eta\,(wx-y)\,x$$

Symbols: $wx$ is the prediction, $wx-y$ is the error (prediction minus target), $x$ is the input, and $\eta$ (eta) is the learning rate. The $\tfrac12$ is there so the 2 from differentiating cancels. If a question writes $L=(wx-y)^2$ with no half, the gradient is $2(wx-y)x$. For a batch of samples, add up (or average) the gradients.
cards.intuition_full: The derivative of a squared error is "error times how much the weight touches the output". If the prediction is too low, the error is negative and so is the gradient for positive $x$. Subtracting a negative number raises $w$, which raises the prediction. So the minus sign in the update always pushes the prediction toward the target. The gradient is large when the error is large, so the steps shrink on their own as you near the minimum. For this squared loss, each step multiplies the distance to the best weight by $1-\eta x^2$. If $\eta x^2$ is below 1 the distance shrinks smoothly. Between 1 and 2 it overshoots but still converges. Above 2 it grows and the method diverges. The rule $\frac{d}{dw}\tfrac12(wx-y)^2=(wx-y)x$ comes from the chain rule.

example.setup: Loss $L=\tfrac12(wx-y)^2$ for one sample $x=2$, $y=6$. Start at $w=1.5$ with learning rate $\eta=0.1$. Take one step, then a second.
steps: Gradient $=(wx-y)\,x=(-3)(2)=-6$. It is negative, so the loss falls if $w$ increases.
Second step: prediction $2.1\cdot2=4.2$, error $-1.8$, gradient $-3.6$, so $w\leftarrow2.1+0.36=2.46$.
The best $w$ is $y/x=3$. Distances to 3: $1.5\to0.9\to0.54$, shrinking by the factor $1-\eta x^2=1-0.4=0.6$ each step.
example.answer: After one step $w=2.1$, after two $w=2.46$. The loss goes $4.5\to1.62\to0.58$.

examples.answer: Sum: $w=1.3$. Mean: $w=1.15$. Read the question to see whether the loss is a sum or a mean, and whether it has a $\tfrac12$.

examples.setup: Same sample $x=2$, $y=6$ and start $w=1.5$, but with a large learning rate $\eta=0.6$. Do three steps.
steps: Step 1: error $-3$, gradient $-6$, $w\leftarrow1.5+3.6=5.1$. It jumped past the best $w=3$.
Step 2: prediction $10.2$, error $4.2$, gradient $8.4$, $w\leftarrow5.1-5.04=0.06$. It jumped back past 3.
Distances from 3: $1.5\to2.1\to2.94\to4.12$. The factor is $1-\eta x^2=1-2.4=-1.4$, which is bigger than 1 in size, so it diverges.
examples.answer: The weight swings back and forth with growing size. A learning rate that is too large ($\eta x^2>2$) makes gradient descent diverge. Keep $\eta x^2<1$ for smooth steps.

cards.why: Gradient descent is how almost every model larger than a line is trained, and the update rule is the same everywhere. In GATE: one gradient step on a small loss, in the style of 2026 DA Q29, where you must get the sign and the factors right.
how: Compute the prediction $wx$ and the error $wx-y$.
Gradient = error times input. Add a factor 2 if the loss has no $\tfrac12$, and add over samples for a batch.
New $w=w-\eta\times$ gradient.
Sanity check: the new prediction should be closer to $y$.
cards.mistake: Adding the gradient instead of subtracting it. That climbs the loss. Watch the sign: a negative gradient means the subtraction increases $w$, which is correct.
edge_cases: A zero gradient makes the update do nothing. You are at a minimum (or a flat spot).
If the objective is linear in $w$, like $f=wx$, the gradient is just $x$ and does not depend on $w$ (2026 DA Q29).
Sum versus mean over a batch changes the step by a factor of the batch size.
Too big a learning rate overshoots and can diverge.
connections: Foundations: Derivatives. The chain rule gives the gradient formula.
Maxima, minima and convexity: squared loss is convex, so descent reaches the global minimum.
Logistic regression uses the same update with error $p-y$, and neural networks repeat it through backpropagation.

check.q: $x=3$, $y=9$, $w=1$, $\eta=0.1$ and loss $\tfrac12(wx-y)^2$. Take one step.
If the loss were $(wx-y)^2$ with no half, how does the gradient change?
check.a: It doubles to $2(wx-y)x$.

check.q: The gradient is $+4$ and $\eta=0.5$. Does $w$ go up or down, and by how much?
check.a: Down, by $0.5\cdot4=2$.

scenes.title: Residuals, squares and SSE for two lines

steps.caption: Four dots. Try the line ŷ = x first. At x = 1, 2, 3, 4 it predicts 1, 2, 3, 4.
Residual = actual minus predicted. The red bars are the gaps: 0, 0, −1 and +1.
Square each gap. The square drawn on a gap has area equal to the squared miss: 0, 0, 1, 1.
Add the squares. SSE = 0 + 0 + 1 + 1 = 2. (Adding the signed gaps would give 0 and hide the misses.)
Squares 0.09, 0.01, 1.21 and 0.49 add up to 1.8. That is smaller than 2, so this line is better.

scenes.title: Through-origin slope: one swing, one formula

steps.caption: The line must pass through the origin, so ŷ = wx. It can only swing steeper or flatter. Three dots to fit.
Multiply each x by its y and add: 1·3 + 2·3 + 3·4 = 3 + 6 + 12 = 21.
Square each x and add: 1 + 4 + 9 = 14.
Divide: w = 21 / 14 = 1.5. This is the best swing for the line.
Check the misses: 1.5, 0 and −0.5 give SSE = 2.25 + 0 + 0.25 = 2.5. Slopes 1 and 2 both give 6.

scenes.title: Slope and intercept from the mean point

steps.caption: Mark the mean point (2.5, 2.5). The best line must pass through it.
Draw a rectangle from the mean point to each dot. Its sides are the distances x − mean x and y − mean y.
Green rectangles (same-sign distances) count as positive area, red as negative: 2.25 + 0.25 − 0.25 + 3.75 = 6. That total is Sxy.
Sxx adds the squared x distances: 2.25 + 0.25 + 0.25 + 2.25 = 5.
Draw ŷ = 1.2x − 0.5. At x = 2.5 it gives 3 − 0.5 = 2.5, so it passes through the mean point.

scenes.title: Residuals balance around the best line

steps.caption: The least-squares line ŷ = 1.2x − 0.5 and its residual arrows: +0.3, +0.1, −1.1, +0.7.
Dots above the line have positive residuals: 0.3 + 0.1 + 0.7 = 1.1.
Dots below the line have negative residuals: just −1.1. Same size, opposite sign.
The two sides cancel: Σe = 1.1 − 1.1 = 0.

scenes.title: R-squared: the line against the lazy guess

steps.caption: The lazy guess: predict the mean, 2.5, for every dot. Its misses are −1.5, −0.5, −0.5 and +2.5.
Square and add the lazy misses: 2.25 + 0.25 + 0.25 + 6.25 = 9. This is SST, the total variation in y.
Now use the fitted line instead. The misses are much smaller: 0.3, 0.1, −1.1, 0.7.
Square and add: 0.09 + 0.01 + 1.21 + 0.49 = 1.8. This is SSE. Compare the bars.
The line leaves 1.8 / 9 = 0.2 of the variation unexplained. So R² = 1 − 0.2 = 0.8.
Hours studied (x) against marks (y). The best line is ŷ = x + 1: slope 1, intercept 1.
Count time in half-hours: x′ = 2x. Every dot slides to double its x. Same data, spread twice as wide.
The new best line is flatter: slope 1/2 = 0.5, intercept still 1. At x′ = 6 it gives 0.5·6 + 1 = 4 marks, same as before.
Add 2 marks to every y. Dots and line both slide up by 2: slope unchanged, intercept 1 → 3.
Rule: scaling x by c divides the slope by c. Shifting y by d adds d to the intercept.

scenes.title: Normal equations: the residual is perpendicular

steps.caption: Each sample is one axis. The feature column x = (3, 1) and the targets y = (1, 3) are arrows. Predictions can only lie on the dashed line (multiples of x). Then $X^\top X=10$ and $X^\top y=6$.
Normal equation: 10 w = 6, so w = 0.6.
The best prediction is the point of the dashed line nearest to y: Xw = 0.6·(3, 1) = (1.8, 0.6).
The leftover is the residual e = y − Xw = (1 − 1.8, 3 − 0.6) = (−0.8, 2.4).
e meets the dashed line at a right angle: e · x = 3(−0.8) + 1(2.4) = −2.4 + 2.4 = 0.

scenes.title: Weights and how many clues fix them

steps.caption: A line ŷ = wx + b has 2 weights: its steepness w and its height b (d + 1 with d = 1 feature). To fix 2 weights you need 2 independent clues.
One dot (2, 3) is only one clue. Many lines fit it exactly: ŷ = 3, ŷ = x + 1, ŷ = 2x − 1 and more.
Two dots with different x, (1, 2) and (3, 5): one line only. Slope (5 − 2)/(3 − 1) = 1.5, b = 2 − 1.5 = 0.5. The matrix $X^\top X$ has determinant $20-16=4$.
Two dots with the same x, (2, 1) and (2, 3): the determinant of $X^\top X$ is $16-16=0$. Every line through (2, 2) has the same SSE of 2.
At x = 2 every one of those lines predicts 2. The weights are not unique, but the prediction is.

scenes.title: More features can only lower training SSE

steps.caption: Intercept only: predict the mean, 2.5, for every dot. SSE = 0.25 + 2.25 + 2.25 + 0.25 = 5.
Add a flag z that is 1 for dots 1 and 3 (the highlighted dots). The fit becomes ŷ = −1 + x + 2z: two parallel lines, one per flag value. Every dot sits on a line, so SSE = 0.
SSE went 5 → 3.2 → 0. It never rose. Setting a new weight to 0 would give back the previous model, so the best fit can only match or beat it.

scenes.title: Gradient steps slide down the loss curve

steps.caption: Start at w = 1.5 on the loss curve L(w) = ½(2w − 6)². Prediction 1.5·2 = 3, target 6, error 3 − 6 = −3.
The slope of the loss here is error × input = (−3)(2) = −6. Negative slope: the valley is to the right.
Step against the slope: w = 1.5 − 0.1·(−6) = 2.1. The loss drops from 4.5 to 1.62.
Second step: prediction 4.2, error −1.8, slope −3.6, so w = 2.1 + 0.36 = 2.46. The step is shorter because the slope is flatter.
Steps keep shrinking as the slope flattens. The valley floor is w = 6/2 = 3, where the slope is 0.
